discovery: The titanium-sapphire laser and passive mode-locking (Kerr-lens and SESAM) that made robust femtosecond lasers possible
motivation: Nearly every ultrafast laboratory in the world runs on the same foundation: a titanium-doped sapphire crystal, passively mode-locked. Peter Moulton invented the Ti:sapphire laser, whose enormous gain bandwidth supports pulses of a few optical cycles and broad tunability. Wilson Sibbett and colleagues discovered self-mode-locking through the optical Kerr effect, a strikingly simple idea that produced femtosecond pulses without any active modulator. Ursula Keller invented the semiconductor saturable absorber mirror, which made mode-locking reliable and self-starting across solid-state, fibre and semiconductor lasers. Together these advances replaced fragile dye lasers with turnkey femtosecond sources. They are the seed oscillators for chirped pulse amplification, and they made possible frequency combs, attosecond science, multiphoton microscopy, ophthalmic surgery and precision micromachining. Several Nobel Prizes have rested on these tools, yet the people who created them have never been recognised.
